CC6 / A CIRCULAR TEXTILE STORY

Old uniforms.
New stories.

A discarded uniform can be the beginning of something useful. Follow its journey from retired workwear to a handmade pouch — and a wider community initiative.

An interactive concept showcase
01 Why it matters

More than
just old clothes.

Uniforms are often retired because of branding, age or organisational requirements, even when portions of the fabric remain usable. Our project asks how those materials might be put to better use.

206,000tonnes of textile & leather waste generated in Singapore, 2024
3%recycling rate for this national waste stream, 2024

National figures cover all textile and leather waste, not uniforms alone. Source: NEA 2024 waste statistics.

From overlooked fabric to new purpose
02 Collection

A better ending
begins with a return.

Start with one corporate partner that already has a uniform-return process. Obtain approval, agree on secure handling, and collect only garments authorised for reuse.

03 People behind the process

Prepared with
purpose.

A social enterprise partner could provide paid, supported work for persons with disabilities and people facing employment barriers, with tasks matched to individual needs and suitable training.

01
Remove identifying features

Handle names, logos and sensitive details according to the uniform owner's rules.

02
Clean and inspect

Prepare only appropriate fabric for safe reuse.

03
Sort by condition

Identify large usable panels, smaller offcuts and unsuitable material.

Proposed paid preparation work
04 After preparation

One material.
Two new purposes.

After inspection, suitable materials can move through two complementary pathways. Tap each image to explore how the fabric could be used.

Pathway 01 / Commercial

Useful everyday products

Larger reusable panels could become hand-stitched pouches and other small-batch products for organisations or buyers.

A local upcycling maker would check fabric suitability, labour time, manufacturing cost and potential customer interest before increasing production.
Pathway 02 / Community

Make together, learn together

Clean, safe fabric offcuts could supply voluntary craft sessions for seniors at participating community centres.

Community partners would need suitable materials, facilitators, accessible session designs and participant feedback; the workshops are not intended as unpaid manufacturing labour.

A circular economy can create both products and participation.

08 Implementation

From a small pilot
to a lasting loop.

Growth should follow evidence. This is the proposed sequence, not a list of completed partnerships.

01

Engage partners

Approach a uniform-owning company, a social enterprise, an upcycling workshop and community centres. Agree on permissions and roles.

02

Test a small batch

Collect, de-identify, sort and prepare fabric. Make trial pouches, set aside workshop offcuts and record yield, cost and feedback.

03

Build participation

Add organisations and community workshops only after pilot capacity, product demand and safe handling are established.

04

Keep the cycle going

Seek repeat orders, stable collection and funding arrangements while tracking useful output and social participation.

A meaningful pilot must address secure identification removal, safe cleaning, fair paid work, product quality, buyer demand and management of unsuitable textiles.
09 Sharely, Not Waste.

Less discarded.
More possible.

Not every retired uniform will become a product. But a thoughtful collection and upcycling system could offer fabric a second use — and create opportunities for people along the way.

This experience visualises a proposal. All photographic scenes are illustrative, not documentation of completed group activities. Any eventual pilot would require real partners, permission and material testing.
